content: A total of 73% of respondents either agreed or fully agreed with the exclusive use of tenofovir or entecavir for the treatment of hepatitis B (Recommendation 1). Additionally, 66% of respondents supported the use of tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) for hepatitis B treatment (Recommendation 2), while 46% agreed or fully agreed with the use of dual therapy involving tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and lamivudine (3TC) (Recommendation 3). Detailed levels of agreement for these recommendations are as follows: 1. For the exclusive use of tenofovir or entecavir, 7% did not agree at all, 2% did not agree, 18% were neutral, 27% agreed, and 46% fully agreed. 2. For the additional option of TAF, 5% did not agree at all, 7% did not agree, 22% were neutral, 24% agreed, and 42% fully agreed. 3. For the additional option of dual therapy with TDF + 3TC, 17% did not agree at all, 2% did not agree, 35% were neutral, 17% agreed, and 29% fully agreed. Regarding access to hepatitis B services, 93% of respondents reported that care is currently available at hospital-based clinics. More than three-quarters (78%) of respondents agreed or fully agreed with providing hepatitis B services at multiple hospital-based clinics, while 61% supported providing these services at primary care clinics. When asked about integrating hepatitis B services with pre-existing HIV clinics or noncommunicable disease clinics, 87% of respondents agreed or fully agreed with integration at HIV clinics, whereas only 51% supported integration at noncommunicable disease clinics. Detailed levels of agreement for simplifying and integrating hepatitis B service delivery are as follows: 1. For providing hepatitis B services at multiple hospital-based clinics, 2% did not agree at all, 2% did not agree, 18% were neutral, 27% agreed, and 51% fully agreed. 2. For providing hepatitis B services at primary care clinics, 7% did not agree at all, 15% did not agree, 17% were neutral, 22% agreed, and 39% fully agreed. 3. For integrating hepatitis B services at HIV clinics, 5% did not agree at all, 3% did not agree, 5% were neutral, 20% agreed, and 67% fully agreed. 4. For integrating hepatitis B services at noncommunicable disease clinics, 5% did not agree at all, 10% did not agree, 34% were neutral, 29% agreed, and 22% fully agreed. Concerning the availability and accessibility of laboratory-based HBV DNA assays and point-of-care HBV DNA assays, 32% of respondents reported the availability or accessibility of laboratory-based testing in their countries. In contrast, only 14% noted the presence or accessibility of point-of-care testing. However, 54% of respondents agreed or fully agreed with the utilization of HBV point-of-care DNA assays as an alternative to laboratory-based HBV DNA assays. Detailed levels of agreement for this recommendation are provided in the corresponding data.
